title: The Dream Books: Nights Written Down as Evidence
subtitle: Dated dream records from Pergamum to London, c. 145–1744
intro: An old Chinese text, the Zhuangzi, tells of a man who dreamed he was a butterfly and on waking could not be sure whether he was a man who had dreamed of a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man. The passage has no date and no diarist, so it stands here only as a question. The people in this chapter did something more practical with the same uncertainty: they wrote their dreams down, with dates, and treated them as evidence about the waking world, then checked what happened next.

The record is uneven, and the forms are named honestly. Aelius Aristides, a sick Greek orator, kept dream notes during his years with Asclepius and later built them into the Sacred Tales. Myōe, a Japanese monk, kept loose dream sheets for forty years, some now in museums. John Dee, Archbishop Laud and Samuel Pepys wrote dreams into diaries beside their daily business. Cardano and Aristides wrote theirs up long afterwards. Descartes's dreams survive only through a biographer's paraphrase and two lines in Leibniz's handwriting. Asiye Hatun of Skopje wrote her dreams as letters to her Sufi sheikh. Swedenborg's pocket journal of 1743–44 is the last and the most continuous.

What joins them is the test. Aristides obeyed a dream and recorded the result on his body. Myōe took a dream as the gods' acceptance of a postponed ceremony. Cardano rewrote a prescription after a dream. Dee prayed to confirm a neighbour's dream. Descartes, a year after his night of dreams, noted that he had begun to understand what it promised. Laud wrote that he was not moved by dreams and kept recording them anyway. Swedenborg asked whether the figure in his vision was really Christ.

The record ledger shows the gaps between dream and telling: hours for Myōe, Dee, Pepys and Swedenborg; decades for Aristides and Cardano; seventy years and another man's pen for Descartes. Several dreams reached print only because someone else chose to print them, a rival prosecutor in Laud's case and a librarian in Swedenborg's.

Gaps: no dated dream entry by Fujiwara no Teika is included, and the Mughal emperor Jahangir's memoirs, which report dreams other people sent him about his accession, are not used as an eye. Most non-European records here survive only in modern translations, so they are summarised rather than quoted. Synesius' treatise On Dreams (c. 404) is included as context: it is the text that tells readers to keep a dream book, not a dream book itself.
calendar_note: Dates before 1582 are Julian. Aristides dated his dreams by local Greek months; the Roman dates follow Charles Behr's conversions and are marked approximate. Myōe used Japanese era names and the lunisolar calendar; the 1225 sheet is converted only to the month. England kept the Julian calendar throughout this chapter, so Dee, Laud and Pepys's Old Style days are shown as written, with sortable New Style dates ten days later; Laud's year began on 25 March, so his January–March entries are given as 1626/7 and 1639/40. Dee sometimes wrote 'veteri stilo' himself. Swedenborg in Holland used the New Style, noting that it was 15 May when the English date was 4 May.
seam: Each of these dreamers treated the night as a source of information about the day, and then checked it: against the body, a ceremony, a patient, a library, a year's work, or scripture. The ledger shows the other part of the story. Most of these dreams reached us through someone else, a copyist, a biographer, a hostile prosecutor or a librarian, and that person decided what counted. Like the cities of The City & the City that occupy the same ground, the dream record and the waking record sit side by side, and these diarists kept moving between them.

eyes.name: Publius Aelius Aristides
eyes.role: Greek orator from Mysia, chronically ill from his mid-twenties; a patient of the healing god Asclepius for some three decades
eyes.side: Greek East of the Roman Empire; devotee of Asclepius
eyes.where: The Asclepieion of Pergamum (145–147) and his estates and Smyrna afterwards
eyes.vantage_label: the patient who kept a dream diary and wrote it up decades later
eyes.form: later firsthand narrative (six 'Sacred Tales', Orations 47–52) drawing on his own dated dream records
eyes.authenticity: The Sacred Tales survive in the manuscript tradition of Aristides' orations. He says he had kept dream records for years but lost many; the first Tale reproduces about six weeks of dated entries from early 166 AD. Dates are given by local Greek months and were converted to Roman equivalents by Charles Behr (1968 study; Brill translation 1981). No English translation before 1929 is known, so all entries here are summaries.
eyes.bio: Aristides was a celebrated rhetorician whose career was broken by illness. He treated every dream as a prescription from Asclepius and then did what it said: fasting, bleeding, cold-river bathing, speaking in public. His Tales are the fullest first-person record of temple healing from antiquity.

sources.title: Johnson, 'Alexander and Demosthenes Side by Side... Integrative Dream Art of Aelius Aristides' (CHS Classics@)
C. A. Behr, Aelius Aristides and the Sacred Tales (1968); P. Aelius Aristides, The Complete Works (Brill, 1981–86)

eyes.name: Synesius of Cyrene
eyes.role: Landowner, philosopher and later bishop of Ptolemais; pupil of Hypatia of Alexandria
eyes.side: Greek Cyrenaica, late Roman Empire; Neoplatonist turning Christian bishop
eyes.where: Cyrene and his estates in Libya
eyes.vantage_label: philosopher writing about his own dreaming
eyes.form: treatise (On Dreams, De insomniis) with autobiographical asides; dated letters
eyes.authenticity: On Dreams survives with his letters; the date c. 404–405 rests on internal evidence and a letter to Hypatia. Context only: it is a treatise, not a diary.
eyes.bio: Synesius argued that the imagination is a mirror in which the soul catches signs of what is real and what is coming, and that every person should keep a record of dreams. He is here as the theorist who told readers to write their dreams down.

sources.title: Synesius, On Dreams (Greek text; English tr. A. Fitzgerald, 1930)

eyes.name: Myōe Kōben
eyes.role: Kegon and Shingon Buddhist monk; founder of Kōzanji at Toganoo, north-west of Kyoto
eyes.where: Kōzanji, Toganoo; earlier hermitages in Kii province
eyes.vantage_label: the monk who wrote the dream down the morning after
eyes.form: dream record (Yume no ki): loose dated and undated sheets
eyes.authenticity: Sheets of the Yume no ki survive at Kōzanji, the Kyoto National Museum (dated pieces of 1207, 1209, 1211), the Metropolitan Museum and the Smithsonian; many were cut up and remounted as hanging scrolls. Kept for about forty years. Studied in English by George Tanabe (Myōe the Dreamkeeper, 1992) and Kawai Hayao; modern translations only, so summaries here.
eyes.bio: Myōe recorded the dreams he wanted to keep, with commentary linking them to his practice and to events in the temple, and sometimes re-read them years later. For him a dream could confirm that a ritual, a vow or a decision was accepted.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum, Section of the Dream Diary, dated 1225 (2014.719.4)
Kyoto National Museum, Kōben Yume no ki (BK559)
Review of G. Tanabe, Myōe the Dreamkeeper (1992), Journal of Asian Studies

eyes.name: Girolamo Cardano
eyes.role: Physician, mathematician and astrologer of Milan, Pavia and Bologna; in old age a pensioner in Rome
eyes.side: Renaissance Italy; Milanese College of Physicians
eyes.vantage_label: the physician recalling his dreams in old age
eyes.authenticity: Written in Rome in 1575–76 and first printed by Gabriel Naudé in Paris in 1643. The only full English version is Jean Stoner's (1930), so summaries only. Cardano also published a commentary on Synesius' dream book (1562).
eyes.bio: Cardano believed he had guiding dreams and a protective spirit, and in old age he set down the dreams he thought had come true. He attaches each to a waking outcome: a patient, a post, a city he would later live in.

sources.title: The Book of My Life (De vita propria), tr. J. Stoner, 1930
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Girolamo Cardano'

eyes.name: John Dee
eyes.role: Mathematician, astrologer and collector of the largest private library in England; adviser at Elizabeth I's court
eyes.side: Elizabethan England; travelled in Central Europe 1583–1589 with Edward Kelley
eyes.where: His house at Mortlake on the Thames; Bohemia and Bremen 1583–89
eyes.vantage_label: noting the dream in an almanac margin
eyes.form: diary (notes in the margins of printed almanacs)
eyes.language: English, with some Latin and English written in Greek letters
eyes.authenticity: The almanacs are in the Ashmolean collections at the Bodleian; edited by J. O. Halliwell for the Camden Society in 1842 (public domain). Dee used Old Style dates and sometimes says so ('veteri stilo').
eyes.bio: Dee's terse margin notes put dreams beside debts, visitors and servants' quarrels. His dreams return again and again to his books, which he feared would be burned or taken; in 1583, while he was abroad, his library was in fact plundered.

sources.title: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. J. O. Halliwell (Camden Society, 1842), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: René Descartes
eyes.role: Twenty-three-year-old gentleman volunteer in the army of Maximilian of Bavaria, wintering in a stove-heated room
eyes.side: France; Catholic Bavarian army at the start of the Thirty Years War
eyes.where: Winter quarters on the Danube (Neuburg or near Ulm, as later accounts say)
eyes.vantage_label: the dreamer, surviving only in fragments
eyes.form: private notebook ('Olympica', within the Cogitationes privatae), lost; fragments survive in a copy
eyes.authenticity: The notebook was listed in the inventory of his papers after his death in Stockholm (1650) and passed to Claude Clerselier in Paris. It is lost. Two short dated Latin notes survive only in Leibniz's copy of c. 1676, printed by Foucher de Careil in 1859; the narrative of the dreams survives only in Baillet's French paraphrase (1691).
eyes.bio: Descartes recorded that on 10 November 1619 he was 'full of enthusiasm' and had found the foundations of a wonderful science; the same night brought three dreams that he interpreted as a call. In his published Discourse (1637) he told the story of that winter without any dreams.

sources.title: 'Descartes's Dreams', The Montreal Review
Cambridge Descartes Lexicon, 'Dreams, Descartes's three'

eyes.name: Adrien Baillet
eyes.role: Priest and librarian to the Lamoignon family in Paris; Descartes's first full biographer
eyes.vantage_label: biographer paraphrasing lost papers seventy years later
eyes.form: biography (secondhand paraphrase): La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes, 1691
eyes.authenticity: Baillet had access to Descartes's papers then held by Clerselier's circle, including the Olympica, and paraphrased the account of the three dreams with his own reflections mixed in. It cannot be checked against the lost original.
eyes.bio: Without Baillet the three dreams would be unknown. He tells them in the third person, and it is often unclear where Descartes's own interpretation ends and Baillet's begins.

sources.title: A. Baillet, La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes (Paris, 1691), book II ch. 1

eyes.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
eyes.role: German philosopher and mathematician, then aged about 30, living in Paris
eyes.side: Holy Roman Empire; Republic of Letters
eyes.vantage_label: the copyist who saved the only firsthand words
eyes.authenticity: Leibniz copied extracts from the Cogitationes privatae from Clerselier's papers; his copy, now in Hanover, was printed in 1859. Dating of the copy to 1675–76 is approximate.
eyes.bio: Leibniz read Descartes critically and copied what he thought worth keeping. His extracts are the only route by which Descartes's own dated words about November 1619 reach us.

sources.title: Foucher de Careil, Œuvres inédites de Descartes (1859); Adam–Tannery vol. X

eyes.name: William Laud
eyes.role: Bishop of St David's, then of Bath and Wells and London; Archbishop of Canterbury from 1633
eyes.side: Church of England; Charles I's court
eyes.vantage_label: the archbishop noting his dreams beside state business
eyes.authenticity: Seized from his rooms in the Tower in 1643 by William Prynne, who printed it with hostile notes as A Breviate of the Life of William Laud (1644) to support the prosecution; Laud said it had been taken against his will. Henry Wharton printed a fuller text in 1695. The diary records about thirty dreams.
eyes.bio: Laud recorded dreams of the king's displeasure, of his rival John Williams, of his dead parents and of being reconciled to Rome. He was troubled by them and also insisted he was not moved by them, a tension that runs through the diary.

sources.title: W. Prynne, A Breviate of the Life of William Laud (1644), EarlyPrint text

eyes.name: William Prynne
eyes.role: Puritan lawyer and pamphleteer, twice mutilated by Star Chamber sentence in the 1630s under Laud's regime; in 1643 charged with preparing the case against him
eyes.vantage_label: the enemy who published another man's dreams
eyes.form: hostile edition of a seized diary
eyes.authenticity: Prynne's Breviate prints Laud's entries, translating the Latin and adding glosses; it is a partisan text but the entries agree in substance with Wharton's later edition.
eyes.bio: Prynne turned a private book of dreams and prayers into evidence. His edition is the first time a set of dated dreams was printed in English to be read against the dreamer.

sources.title: A Breviate of the Life of William Laud (1644)

eyes.name: Asiye Hatun of Üsküp
eyes.role: Woman of Skopje (Üsküp), disciple of a Halveti Sufi sheikh
eyes.vantage_label: the disciple who sent her dreams to her sheikh
eyes.authenticity: A single surviving manuscript of her dream reports addressed to her sheikh, studied and edited by Cemal Kafadar ('Mütereddit bir mutasavvıf: Üsküplü Asiye Hatun'un rüya defteri 1641–1643'; reprinted 2009). Described as the only first-person narrative by an Ottoman woman before the Tanzimat yet published. Modern edition only: summaries.
eyes.bio: Asiye Hatun wrote down her dreams and sent them for interpretation, treating them as a channel between herself, her teacher and the divine. Kafadar's title calls her a 'hesitant' or doubting mystic: the record shows her questioning what the dreams meant.

sources.title: Bozkurt and Günay-Erkol, 'Dreams beyond Control: Women and Writing in the Ottoman Empire since Asiye Hatun's Diary' (2014)
Kafadar 2009 essay cited in DergiPark article

eyes.name: Samuel Pepys
eyes.role: Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board, aged 32
eyes.where: The Navy Office in Seething Lane and, in the plague, Greenwich
eyes.vantage_label: the diarist writing the morning after
eyes.authenticity: Written in Shelton's shorthand; deciphered in 1819–22 and first printed, expurgated, in 1825. Text here from Wheatley's edition via Project Gutenberg.
eyes.bio: Pepys rarely records dreams, which makes the one of 15 August 1665 stand out: written during the worst weeks of the Great Plague, it turns a pleasant dream into a thought about death.

sources.title: Diary of Samuel Pepys, August 1665 (Wheatley ed.), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Emanuel Swedenborg
eyes.role: Swedish mining assessor, anatomist and natural philosopher, aged 55–56, abroad to publish his Regnum Animale
eyes.side: Sweden; Lutheran; visiting the Moravians in London
eyes.where: The Hague, Delft, Amsterdam, then London
eyes.authenticity: An octavo pocket book of 104 written pages covering July 1743 to October 1744; it surfaced in 1849, was bought by the Royal Library in Stockholm in 1858 and printed by G. E. Klemming in 1859 in 99 copies. English translations by Wilkinson (1860), Tafel (1877, expurgated) and C. Th. Odhner (1918, restoring the omitted passages in Latin).
eyes.bio: Swedenborg read his dreams as coded comments on his scientific work and his soul, interpreting symbols entry by entry. The journal records the spring in which he turned from anatomy towards the visionary theology of his later life.

sources.title: Swedenborg's Journal of Dreams (tr. Odhner, 1918), Public Domain Review
The Swedenborg Epic, ch. 23, 'The Turning Point'
'The Erotic Dreams of Emanuel Swedenborg', Public Domain Review

entries.headline: An invalid orator moves into the god's sanctuary
entries.digest: After an illness that wrecked a journey to Rome in late 143, Aristides took up residence at the healing sanctuary of Asclepius at Pergamum. For about two years he lived by the god's dream instructions, alongside other wealthy patients who compared notes on their dreams.
entries.source_note: CHS Classics@ article (residence 145–147, citing Sacred Tales 4.15); Behr's chronology

entries.headline: Ordered in a dream to start speaking again
entries.digest: Midway through his stay, Aristides recorded, the god urged him in dreams to return to oratory, which illness had stopped. He treated the instruction as a test of the god's power over his body and began to compose and declaim again.
entries.source_note: Sacred Tales 4.15, as cited by the CHS Classics@ article

entries.headline: Crowned as Demosthenes in a dream
entries.digest: He dreamed of being crowned, in the persona of Demosthenes, at the Olympieion, and of seeing Alexander and Demosthenes laid in a shared tomb. He read these as the god ranking him among the great orators and as encouragement to persist in public speaking.
entries.source_note: Sacred Tales 4.48–49 via CHS Classics@ article ('sometime around 147 CE')

entries.headline: Surviving the great plague
entries.digest: When the plague later called Antonine swept the eastern provinces, Aristides fell ill with it. He survived and credited dreams sent by the gods with his recovery, after which his devotion to Asclepius deepened.
entries.source_note: Biographical summaries of the Sacred Tales (Book 2); Behr chronology

entries.date_display: 11 January 166 AD (Behr's conversion of a local Greek date)
entries.headline: Captured by Parthians, who try to brand him
entries.digest: The first Sacred Tale opens a dated run of dream entries. In this one Parthians took him prisoner and one tried to brand him. At this moment Rome really was at war with Parthia, and the war is part of his dreamscape.
entries.source_note: Sacred Tales 1.9, date as given in the CHS Classics@ article following Behr
entries.form: dream diary entries reproduced in later narrative

entries.headline: Told not to kiss the emperor
entries.digest: He dreamed he saw the Roman emperor and that Asclepius instructed him not to kiss him. As usual, Aristides recorded the instruction as precisely as a doctor's order and worked out what it meant for his conduct and treatment.
entries.source_note: Sacred Tales 1.23 via CHS Classics@ article
entries.form: dream diary entries reproduced in later narrative

entries.headline: A dream of peace between Rome and Parthia
entries.digest: He dreamed that the Roman emperor and the Parthian king made peace. Rome did end the war with Parthia that year. The modern discussion gives the day of the dream inconsistently, so only the month is shown here.
entries.source_note: Sacred Tales 1.36–39; CHS Classics@ article gives both 4 February and 'the twelfth'
entries.form: dream diary entries reproduced in later narrative

entries.headline: Two emperors, an elder and a younger
entries.digest: A variant dream showed him two Roman emperors, one older and one younger, matching the joint rule of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. The emperors, the war and his own body run together in these weeks of entries.
entries.source_note: Sacred Tales 1.47–49 via CHS Classics@ article
entries.form: dream diary entries reproduced in later narrative

entries.headline: Writing the Sacred Tales from his records
entries.digest: About twenty-five years after Pergamum, Aristides began composing the Sacred Tales. He explains that he could not tell everything, because many of his old dream records were lost, and he reconstructed what he could around the dated entries that survived.
entries.source_note: Biographical summaries (composition begun c. 171); Behr 1968

entries.headline: A philosopher tells his readers to keep a dream book
entries.digest: In On Dreams Synesius argued that imagination is a mirror for signs from reality and the future, and urged everyone to record their dreams, waking and sleeping impressions alike, as one would keep a chronicle. He says his own dreams had helped him in his work, and in a letter to Hypatia he describes writing the treatise quickly, as if under divine prompting.
entries.source_note: Synesius, De insomniis; Letters (to Hypatia); date from internal evidence

entries.headline: Cutting off his ear before the Buddha
entries.digest: At about twenty-three, Myōe cut off his own right ear as a sign of renunciation. Afterwards he is said to have had a vision of the bodhisattva Monju, which he took as confirmation of the act. His dream record, kept from his youth, grows fuller from these years.
entries.source_note: Tricycle review of Kawai (ear-cutting at 23); Tanabe 1992; the episode is known chiefly through his disciples' biography

entries.headline: A dream companion turns out to be a Kasuga deity
entries.digest: On one surviving sheet Myōe records meeting two acquaintances in a dream, one of whom proved to be a god of Kasuga Shrine in Nara. He sketched three peaks beside the text, the three mountains of Kasuga, with the wooded hills of his own temple below.
entries.source_note: Metropolitan Museum 2014.719.3, dated ca. 1203–10

entries.headline: Drawing lots on going to India
entries.digest: Myōe twice planned a pilgrimage to India, the land of the Buddha. After an oracle of the Kasuga deity in 1203 told him not to go, he tried again in 1205 and, according to the temple's account, put the question to lots drawn before sacred images; the lots said no, and he stayed.
entries.source_note: Tricycle review (two failed attempts at an India pilgrimage); details from Tanabe 1992 and Kasuga records

entries.date_display: 16th day of the 8th month, Karoku 1 (1225); about September 1225 in the Julian calendar
entries.headline: A typhoon postpones a dedication; the gods arrive in dreams
entries.digest: On this unusually fully dated sheet, Myōe notes that a typhoon put off the ceremony to dedicate three shrines at Kōzanji to Byakkō, the Kasuga deity and Zenmyō. That night he had two dreams in which he met people he took to be those three deities in human form, as if the dedication had been accepted after all.
entries.source_note: Metropolitan Museum 2014.719.4; Western date approximate

entries.headline: Climbing a sheer mountain to a boy in grey
entries.digest: Cardano dreamed he climbed a mountain to a dangerous summit and found a cottage with a boy of about twelve in an ash-coloured suit. Forty years later he read it as a forecast of his fame and his hardships, his imprisonment and the ruin of his son.
entries.source_note: De vita propria ch. 37 (Stoner tr. 1930)

entries.headline: A serpent dream changes a prescription
entries.digest: After dreaming of a huge serpent that threatened him, Cardano was called to the seven-year-old son of Count Camillo Borromeo. Remembering the dream, he tore up his first prescription and wrote another. The boy died next day, and Cardano credited the dream with saving him from blame.
entries.source_note: De vita propria ch. 33

entries.headline: Woken to save his son Aldo
entries.digest: In Pavia he was woken by a nurse who told him his infant son Aldo was dying. He gave a powder of pearls and gems, the child vomited, took a second dose and recovered within three days. He set the episode among his dreams and marvels.
entries.source_note: De vita propria ch. 37

entries.headline: A city called Bacchetta
entries.digest: He dreamed of a festive city named Bacchetta, with a gilded house and five palaces. Years later, living in Rome, he found such a house and decided the dream had shown him the last stage of his life.
entries.source_note: De vita propria ch. 37

entries.headline: An old man audits his dreams
entries.digest: In his last years in Rome, Cardano wrote his autobiography, giving chapters to his guardian spirit and to dreams that came true. He did not publish it; Gabriel Naudé printed it in Paris in 1643.
entries.source_note: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Stoner 1930 introduction

entries.headline: Dreaming his skin embroidered with crosses
entries.digest: Dee noted his dream of being naked, his skin worked all over like a tufted fabric with blue and red crosses. The note sits among household business, with no interpretation added.
entries.quote: my dream of being naked, and my skyn all overwrowght with work like some kinde of tuft mockado, with crosses blew and red
entries.source_note: Private Diary, ed. Halliwell 1842, s.v. 1579 Sept. 10th

entries.headline: A neighbour's repeated dream, confirmed by prayer
entries.digest: Harry Prise of Lewisham came to Dee with a dream he kept having. Dee prayed that night and recorded that the dream was confirmed and further instruction given: the dream of another person checked by his own practice.
entries.quote: told of his dreames often repeated, and uppon my prayer to God this night, his dreame was confirmed, and better instruction given.
entries.source_note: Private Diary, ed. Halliwell 1842, s.v. 1581 Feb. 11th

entries.headline: Dreaming his own death and the burning of his books
entries.digest: Dee dreamed he was dead and his bowels taken out, yet he walked and talked with people, among them the Lord Treasurer, who had come to burn his books and looked sourly at him. His library was the work of his life, and the fear of losing it recurs in his dreams.
entries.quote: Saterday night I dremed that I was deade, and afterward my bowels wer taken out. I walked and talked with diverse, and among other with the Lord Thresorer who was com to my howse to burn my bokes when I was dead, and thought he loked sourely on me.
entries.source_note: Private Diary, ed. Halliwell 1842, s.v. 1582 Nov. 24th (Saturday confirmed by calendar)

entries.headline: Edward Kelley comes to take his books
entries.digest: Waiting in Bremen on his way home after years in Bohemia, Dee recorded a terrible dream towards daybreak that his former partner Edward Kelley would seize his books by force. When he reached Mortlake that December he found his library had been plundered in his absence.
entries.quote: my terrible dream that Mr. Kelly wold by force bereave me of my bokes, toward daybreak.
entries.source_note: Private Diary, ed. Halliwell 1842, s.v. 1589 Aug. 2nd ('veteri stilo')

entries.headline: Two nights dreaming of Kelley
entries.digest: Back in England for over three years, Dee noted that on two nights running he dreamed much of Kelley, as though he were living familiarly in Dee's house with his wife and brother. Kelley was then far away in Bohemia.
entries.quote: these two nights I dremed much of Mr. Kelly, as if he wer in my howse familiar with his wife and brother.
entries.source_note: Private Diary, ed. Halliwell 1842, s.v. 1593 March 12th and 13th

entries.headline: A vow made in thanks
entries.digest: According to Baillet, Descartes was so shaken that he prayed for guidance and vowed a pilgrimage to the shrine of Our Lady at Loreto. Whether or when he made it rests on Baillet alone.
entries.source_note: Baillet 1691, II.1

entries.headline: 'Full of enthusiasm': the foundations of a wonderful science
entries.digest: In his private notebook Descartes dated the day he became full of enthusiasm and found the foundations of a wonderful science. The note survives only in Leibniz's copy; the notebook itself is lost.
entries.quote: X Novembris 1619, cum plenus forem Enthusiasmo, et mirabilis scientiae fundamenta reperirem
entries.source_note: Cogitationes privatae in Leibniz's copy, printed by Foucher de Careil (1859); Adam–Tannery X

entries.headline: Three dreams: whirlwind, thunderclap, the book of poets
entries.digest: Baillet relates that Descartes, after a day of intense thought by a stove, dreamed of phantoms and a whirlwind driving him towards a college chapel, where someone offered him a melon; then of a crack like thunder and sparks filling the room; then of a dictionary and an anthology of poets open at Ausonius' line asking what road in life to follow. Before he woke he realised he was dreaming and began to interpret it: the dictionary as the sciences, the poets as wisdom. He decided the Spirit of Truth had opened the sciences to him.
entries.source_note: Baillet, Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes (1691), II.1, paraphrasing the lost Olympica; summary via The Montreal Review

entries.headline: A year later: beginning to understand
entries.digest: Exactly a year and a day after the dreams, a second dated note in the same notebook says he began to understand the foundation of a wonderful discovery. The dreamer is checking the promise of the dream against his own progress.
entries.quote: XI Novembris 1620, coepi intelligere fundamentum Inventi mirabilis
entries.source_note: Cogitationes privatae, Leibniz's copy; Adam–Tannery X

entries.place: Court, during the summer of plague and Parliament
entries.headline: Buckingham in a dream
entries.digest: Bishop Laud recorded a dream that the Duke of Buckingham, his patron and the king's favourite, came into his bed and treated him with great affection, while others came into the room and saw. Laud wrote it down in Latin; Prynne later printed it in English to damage him.
entries.quote: that night in a dream, the Duke of Buckingham seemed to me to ascend into my bed; where he carried himself with much love towards me
entries.source_note: Prynne, Breviate (1644), under 'An. 1625'

entries.headline: Williams in iron chains, then riding away
entries.digest: Towards morning Laud dreamed that John Williams, Bishop of Lincoln and his rival, came in iron chains, then returned free of them, leapt on a horse and rode off where Laud could not catch him. Williams was in fact later prosecuted and imprisoned in the Tower (1637), and released in 1640.
entries.quote: Towards the morning I dreamed that the Bishop of Lincoln I know not with whom, came with Iron chains, but returning freed from them, he leaped upon a horse, departed, neither could I overtake him
entries.source_note: Prynne, Breviate (1644), under 'Anno 1626'; year assumed to begin 25 March, so January falls in 1627 N.S.

entries.headline: Dreaming he had gone over to Rome
entries.digest: Laud dreamed he had been reconciled to the Church of Rome, was distressed by the scandal, set out to confess and ask pardon, and pushed past a priest who tried to stop him. On waking the impression was so strong he could hardly believe it had been a dream: a striking record for a man later accused of popery.
entries.quote: I felt such impressions, that I could scarce believe I had dreamed.
entries.source_note: Prynne, Breviate (1644), under 'Anno 1626', placed before 'Anno 1627'

entries.headline: The king, offended, casts him off
entries.digest: Now Archbishop, Laud recorded a Friday-night dream in which Charles I was offended with him and would cast him off. The fear of royal disfavour is the diary's commonest dream theme.
entries.quote: I dreamed marvellously that the King was offended with me, and would cast me off
entries.source_note: Prynne, Breviate (1644), under 'Anno. 1636'; Friday confirmed by calendar

entries.headline: His father returns: 'I am not moved with dreams'
entries.digest: Laud dreamed that his father, dead some forty-six years, came to him. He added that he was not moved by dreams, while still writing this one down, as he had written down dozens before.
entries.quote: At night, I dreamed that my Father (who died 46. years since) came to me
entries.source_note: Prynne, Breviate (1644), under 'Anno 1639'; N.S. year inferred

entries.headline: Dreams sent to a sheikh
entries.digest: Over about two years Asiye Hatun wrote her dreams down and sent them to her Halveti sheikh, asking what they meant. In them she meets her teacher and holy figures, and receives answers to questions she put while awake; the letters treat dreams as real communications.
entries.source_note: Kafadar, 'Üsküplü Asiye Hatun'un rüya defteri 1641–1643' (2009 reprint); Bozkurt and Günay-Erkol 2014

entries.headline: A hesitant mystic
entries.digest: The record does not show simple belief. Asiye Hatun doubts, questions and waits for confirmation, and her writing reflects a culture in which a woman's dreams, or a poor person's, were thought less reliable than a man's. Her dreams had to be tested by someone with more authority before they counted.
entries.source_note: Kafadar 2009; DergiPark article citing Kafadar on the unequal status of dreams

entries.headline: The prisoner's diary is taken
entries.digest: With Laud a prisoner in the Tower, Prynne searched his rooms and carried off his papers, including the diary, to build the impeachment case. Laud complained that even his private book of devotions was taken.
entries.source_note: Breviate (1644) preface and standard accounts of the Laud trial

entries.headline: Printing the archbishop's dreams
entries.digest: Prynne published the diary as A Breviate of the Life of William Laud, with glosses steering readers to see ambition and popery in it. The dream entries, written for no one, were now read publicly against the man who dreamed them, months before his execution in January 1645.
entries.source_note: A Breviate of the Life of William Laud (London, 1644)

entries.headline: The best dream ever dreamt, in the plague time
entries.digest: Walking to Greenwich at four in the morning, Pepys remembered a dream of Lady Castlemaine in his arms, and that in the dream he had known it could not be real. The thought led him to Hamlet: if the dead could dream such dreams, there would be less need to fear death during this plague, which was then killing thousands of Londoners a week.
entries.quote: what a happy thing it would be if when we are in our graves (as Shakespeere resembles it) we could dream, and dream but such dreams as this, that then we should not need to be so fearful of death, as we are this plague time.
entries.source_note: Diary, 15 August 1665 (Wheatley ed., Project Gutenberg)

entries.headline: Copying a dead man's notebook
entries.digest: In Paris, Leibniz copied extracts from Descartes's private notes, held by Clerselier, including the two dated November notes. Neither he nor anyone else copied the full Olympica, which was later lost.
entries.source_note: Foucher de Careil (1859); Adam–Tannery X

entries.headline: The dreams appear in print
entries.digest: Baillet's two-volume life of Descartes put the three dreams before the public for the first time, seventy-two years after the night. Descartes's own published account of 1619, in the Discourse on Method, had not mentioned them.
entries.source_note: Baillet, Vie (Paris, 1691)

entries.headline: Face to face with Christ
entries.digest: After reading about Moses' miracles and doubting, Swedenborg went to bed at ten. Half an hour later he heard a roar like wind, was thrown to the floor trembling, and found himself, as he wrote, face to face with Christ, who asked if he had 'a bill of health'. Half-awake afterwards, he weighed whether the figure was really Christ, mindful of the instruction to test spirits, and concluded it was.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams, Easter 1744; The Swedenborg Epic ch. 23

entries.headline: Impure to the world, pure in themselves
entries.digest: In another entry he recorded a dream he admitted would look impure to worldly eyes but insisted was pure in itself. The erotic dreams were later cut from the 1877 English translation and restored in Latin in 1918.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams, 24 April 1744; Public Domain Review essay

entries.headline: Outside the Moravian chapel
entries.digest: Newly arrived in London, he lodged among Moravians in Fetter Lane and visited their chapel. He wrote that it might not yet be permitted for him to join their brotherhood, and kept apart.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams; The Swedenborg Epic ch. 23

entries.headline: A palace with an open window
entries.digest: He dreamed of a large palace overlooking a fig grove and a moat, and wanted a room in one wing where a window stood open. He suggested the palace stood for the plan of his work, then in progress.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams; The Swedenborg Epic ch. 23

entries.headline: A voice: hold your tongue
entries.digest: Deep in thought over his work, he heard a voice threaten to strike him if he did not hold his tongue. He took it as a warning against burying himself in study, especially on Sundays and in the evenings.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams; The Swedenborg Epic ch. 23

entries.headline: A dream gives the title of a new book
entries.digest: A dream gave him the title for a new 'divine book' on the worship and love of God, which became De cultu et amore Dei (1745). He sensed it would come from a different love than his earlier science, and nearly abandoned it before deciding to go on.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams; The Swedenborg Epic ch. 23

entries.headline: Leading the girl away from science
entries.digest: He dreamed that a beautiful girl fell into a friend's arms in a long passage, would not say whether she knew him, and was led away by him. He read her as his scientific work, which he was drawing towards spiritual writing instead: one of the last entries before the journal ends.
entries.source_note: Journal of Dreams; The Swedenborg Epic ch. 23

convergences.label: Descartes's night of three dreams
convergences.note: One night reaches us through three hands: Descartes's own two-line note (in Leibniz's copy), Leibniz who copied it, and Baillet who paraphrased the lost full narrative. The firsthand line records enthusiasm and a discovery; only the secondhand version tells the dreams.

convergences.label: Private dream books cross into other hands
convergences.note: In 1643 Prynne seized Laud's diary of dreams in the Tower, and Naudé printed Cardano's long-unpublished autobiography in Paris, with its dreams that came true. In Skopje, Asiye Hatun's surviving letters, sent to her sheikh for judgement, end in about the same year. In each case another person decides what the dreams mean.

convergences.label: The Easter dream at Delft
convergences.note: A single-witness date, included as the end point: the last and fullest dream journal in the chapter, kept by a scientist who tested his night experiences against scripture and his own work.

ties.note: Baillet built his 1691 biography on Descartes's papers, including the lost Olympica, and is the only source for the three dreams.
Leibniz read Descartes's unpublished notes in Clerselier's keeping in Paris and copied the dated November fragments.
Laud's Star Chamber had Prynne mutilated in the 1630s; in 1643–44 Prynne seized and published Laud's diary for the prosecution.
Cardano published a commentary on Synesius' dream book in 1562, alongside his own dream lore.
Cardano passed through London in 1552 on his return from Scotland; Dee later recalled meeting him.
Prynne, by then a Member of Parliament, appears repeatedly in Pepys's diary of the 1660s.
Swedenborg's natural philosophy drew on Leibniz and his follower Christian Wolff before his turn to dream and vision in 1744.
Swedenborg's early cosmology in his Principia (1734) worked within and against Cartesian physics, a generation before his own dream journal.

threads_out.note: Descartes's night of 10 November 1619 is the classic early case of a new idea of knowledge credited to a dream, though only the secondhand telling keeps the dreams themselves.
Laud's diary, seized and printed by Prynne in 1644, and Pepys's shorthand diary, unread until 1819, show what happens when private dream records reach readers they were not written for.
Descartes dreamed his three dreams in winter quarters as a volunteer with the Bavarian army in the first campaigns of the Thirty Years War.
Pepys's dream of 15 August 1665, written in the worst weeks of the Great Plague, comes from the same diary that records the Fire a year later.

Myōe and Swedenborg are twelfth- and eighteenth-century counterparts to Hildegard of Bingen: religious figures who wrote down their visions and treated them as instructions they had to test and act on.
